title: Article 123 — Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament

content.overview: Article 123 — Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament. Complete constitutional treatise with procedural anchors, cases, and chamber drafting blueprints.

content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 123 of the Constitution of India is titled “Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament”. It forms an integral component of The Union (Articles 52–151), located within the “Parliament” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.

(2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but every such Ordinance—

(a) shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or, if before the expiration of that period resolutions disapproving it are passed by both Houses, upon the passing of the second of those resolutions; and

(b) may be withdrawn at any time by the President.

Explanation.—Where the Houses of Parliament are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the later of those dates for the purposes of this clause.

(3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which Parliament would not under this Constitution be competent to enact, it shall be void. 1(4) [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted CHAPTER IV.—THE UNION JUDICIARY

Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 123 as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. Key aspect: D.C. Wadhwa (1987) condemned re-promulgation as a fraud on the Constitution. Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) held re-promulgation generally unconstitutional.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish
1. (1) If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.
2. (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but every such Ordinance—
3. (a) shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or, if before the expiration of that period resolutions disapproving it are passed by both Houses, upon the passing of the second of those resolutions; and
4. (b) may be withdrawn at any time by the President.
5. Explanation.—Where the Houses of Parliament are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the later of those dates for the purposes of this clause.
6. (3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which Parliament would not under this Constitution be competent to enact, it shall be void. 1(4) [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted CHAPTER IV.—THE UNION JUDICIARY

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 123 is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

examples.body: State action or statutory exercise strictly satisfies the conditions laid down under Article 123 (Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament). The authority acts within constitutional bounds, respects procedural fairness, and advances the constitutional objective of Parliament. Outcome: Action is held valid and enforceable by the Court.

The action is tainted by manifest arbitrariness, lacks legislative competence, or ignores mandatory safeguards. Outcome: The Court strikes down the measure or issues a writ of certiorari / mandamus.

hypotheticals.question: Examine the constitutional validity of the impugned directive in light of Article 123 and settled Supreme Court jurisprudence. What relief, if any, can be granted?
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Scrutinize the constitutional source of power: Does Article 123 grant plenary power, or is it conditioned by express safeguards, legislative competence, or fundamental rights?
2. Apply the doctrine of ultra vires and manifest arbitrariness: If the directive creates arbitrary exceptions or bypasses statutory provisions, it violates Article 14 and the mandate of Article 123.
3. Examine procedural compliance: Substantive and procedural requirements under the Constitution cannot be waived on mere grounds of administrative convenience.
4. Balance public interest vs constitutional discipline: Constitutional limitations always prevail over executive fiat.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Case Brief & Legal Assessment: Scope and Application of Article 123 (Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 123 (Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 123 is situated in The Union (Articles 52–151), governing the “Parliament” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.
2. (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but every such Ordinance—
3. (a) shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or, if before the expiration of that period resolutions disapproving it are passed by both Houses, upon the passing of the second of those resolutions; and
4. (b) may be withdrawn at any time by the President.
5. Explanation.—Where the Houses of Parliament are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the later of those dates for the purposes of this clause.
6. (3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which Parliament would not under this Constitution be competent to enact, it shall be void. 1(4) [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted CHAPTER IV.—THE UNION JUDICIARY

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 123:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 123 stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 123 of the Constitution of India, titled “Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within The Union (Articles 52–151), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 123 reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.
(a) Limb 2: (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but every such Ordinance—
(a) Limb 3: (a) shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or, if before the expiration of that period resolutions disapproving it are passed by both Houses, upon the passing of the second of those resolutions; and
(a) Limb 4: (b) may be withdrawn at any time by the President.
(a) Limb 5: Explanation.—Where the Houses of Parliament are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the later of those dates for the purposes of this clause.
(a) Limb 6: (3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which Parliament would not under this Constitution be competent to enact, it shall be void. 1(4) [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted CHAPTER IV.—THE UNION JUDICIARY
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 123 must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 123 across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 123:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 123;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 123 without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 123?
Rule: Under Article 123, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 123 remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

enhancement.definition: Article 123 empowers the President of India to promulgate Ordinances during the recess of Parliament when circumstances exist rendering it necessary to take immediate action. An Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but is a temporary emergency power designed for unforeseen exigencies, subject to mandatory parliamentary approval upon reassembly and strict judicial review against colorable executive overreach.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The Ordinance-making power is an extraordinary legislative power vested in the Executive to meet urgent, unforeseen situations when Parliament is not in session. It cannot be used as a substitute for ordinary parliamentary law-making or to bypass democratic debate; repeated re-promulgation of ordinances without legislative approval is a fraud on the Constitution.

Article 123 of the Constitution of India
Parallel power of the State Governor under Article 213

Subject to judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 (R.K. Garg; D.C. Wadhwa; Krishna Kumar Singh)
essentialIngredients: Recess of Parliament: Can be promulgated only when either House of Parliament (or both Houses) is not in session.
Subjective Satisfaction of Immediate Action: President must be satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action.

Co-extensive with Legislative Competence: An Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but is subject to the same constitutional limitations — it cannot enact what Parliament is incompetent to enact, nor violate Part III Fundamental Rights.
Mandatory Parliamentary Laying: Must be laid before both Houses of Parliament upon reassembly.
Temporal Expiration: Ceases to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or earlier if disapproved by resolutions of both Houses.
Withdrawal Power: May be withdrawn by the President at any time.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Article 123 balances the need for prompt executive responses to sudden national crises with the democratic imperative of parliamentary legislative supremacy.

### 1. Nature of the Power
In *A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982)* and *R.K. Garg v. Union of India (1981)*, the Supreme Court held that the Ordinance power is not an executive power but an extraordinary legislative power. The President acts on the aid and advise of the Council of Ministers under Article 74.

### 2. Judicial Review of Presidential Satisfaction
- The 38th Amendment (1975) made the President's satisfaction final and non-justiciable. This was repealed by the 44th Amendment (1978).
- In *Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017)*, a 7-judge Constitution Bench held that the President's satisfaction under Article 123 is amenable to judicial review. The Court does not examine the adequacy of reasons, but investigates whether relevant material existed and whether the power was exercised mala fide or for a collateral purpose.

### 3. Re-promulgation as a Fraud on the Constitution
In *D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987)*, the Supreme Court discovered that the State Government of Bihar had kept 256 ordinances alive for up to 14 years by mechanically re-promulgating them without tabling them before the legislature. The Court struck down this practice as a subversion of the democratic legislative process.
In *Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)*, the 7-judge bench went further, ruling that:
1. The requirement to lay an ordinance before Parliament is **mandatory**; failure to lay is a constitutional infraction.
2. Re-promulgation without legislative debate is a **fraud on the Constitution**.
3. Rights, privileges, or liabilities created under an expired or disapproved ordinance do not automatically survive permanently; they survive only if reversing them is impossible or contrary to public interest.
examples: Emergency Response During Recess: While Parliament is prorogued between sessions, a catastrophic pandemic breaks out requiring emergency powers to requisition medical facilities and regulate drug supplies. Promulgation of an Ordinance under Article 123 is a valid and legitimate exercise of power to meet an unforeseen emergency.

Subverting Legislative Scrutiny (Re-promulgation): An Ordinance imposing controversial market cess fails to secure support in the Rajya Sabha and Parliament prorogues without passing it. The Executive immediately re-promulgates the identical ordinance during the inter-session recess. Applying Krishna Kumar Singh, the re-promulgation is unconstitutional and a fraud on the Constitution.
distinctions: Article 123 (President) vs Article 213 (Governor): Article 123 covers matters within Union/Concurrent competence across India; Article 213 covers State/Concurrent matters within a State, and requires prior Presidential instruction for certain sensitive classes of bills.

Ordinance vs Act of Parliament: An Act of Parliament is permanent legislation enacted after democratic debate and voting; an Ordinance is temporary legislation created unilaterally by the Executive, expiring automatically 6 weeks post-reassembly unless ratified.
problemApplication: Issue: Parliament is in session. The Lok Sabha passes a Bill, but the Rajya Sabha adjourns for the day without voting. The President immediately prorogues the Rajya Sabha and promulgates the Bill as an Ordinance on grounds of urgency. Is the Ordinance valid?

Rule: Under Article 123(1), an ordinance can be promulgated only when either House of Parliament is not in session, but proroguing a House solely to circumvent legislative debate and pass an ordinance is a colorable exercise of power.
Application: Deliberately engineering the prorogation of one House to bypass legislative scrutiny is mala fide and an abuse of constitutional authority.
Counterargument: The Government argues that technically the Rajya Sabha was not in session, satisfying the literal wording of Article 123(1).

Conclusion: While technically permissible if genuine emergency exists, if proven to be a colorable device to bypass parliamentary opposition, the ordinance is vulnerable to judicial invalidation for mala fide exercise of power.
